summary: Describes an architecture for notifications and filtering that make email more usable on mobile and constrained devices. Notifications tell the client about significant events, such as new mail arriving, so it can react by fetching what matters.

plainLanguage.summary: Your phone can buzz when a letter arrives instead of checking constantly. This note explains how mail systems send those alerts.

questions: how do email notifications work for mobile
subtitle: How email systems can tell phones and other constrained clients that something interesting happened, without constant polling.

tldr.problem: Mobile and other constrained devices need to learn about significant mailbox events such as new mail, and to see only the messages that matter, without wasting bandwidth, memory or screen space.
tldr.mechanism: The Lemonade architecture defines four kinds of filters, in-IMAP notifications through IDLE or NOTIFY, out-of-IMAP notifications, and server-to-server state change events sent from the mail system to a separate notification system.
tldr.outcome: A client can be told about events and then connect to resynchronize. The RFC is Informational architecture text and defines no new protocol.

today: RFC 5551 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an architecture rather than a protocol, and it builds on the Lemonade Profile in RFC 5550.

sections.title: Notifications for Lemonade
sections.content:
The Lemonade (Enhancements to Internet email to Support Diverse Service Environments) work identified a need for notification and filtering mechanisms for use with IMAP. Notifications make a client aware of significant events, such as new mail arriving, so it can react by fetching interesting mail immediately. Filtering reduces the visible mail to the messages that meet some criteria for being interesting.

External groups, including the Open Mobile Alliance, also asked for these features. Their requirements cover within-IMAP ("inband") and out-of-IMAP ("outband") notifications from server to client. The RFC also covers server-to-server notifications and how they fit into the same picture.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones have small screens and slow connections, so they should only be told about the mail that matters and only when something happens.

sections.title: The Four Filters
sections.content:
The logical architecture follows the Lemonade Profile (RFC 5550). It defines four categories of filter:

  • AF, Administrative Filters, created by mail administration to apply policies, content filtering, virus protection and spam filtering.
  • DF, Deposit Filters, run when new mail is deposited and can be written as Sieve filters.
  • VF, View Filters, define which messages are important to a client, and may be implemented as pseudo-virtual mailboxes. Clients can use them to restrict what they synchronize.
  • NF, Notification Filters, decide when out-of-IMAP notifications go to the client. They live either in the message store or in a separate notification server, but not both.

Clients manage NF and DF inside the mail store with a Sieve management protocol, and manage VF through pseudo-virtual mailboxes. Using Sieve for DF or NF will likely need the enotify and variables extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of four helpers sorting your mail. One removes junk, one files new letters, one chooses what your phone shows, and one decides when to ring the bell.

sections.title: Inband and Outband Notifications
sections.content:
For in-IMAP (inband) notifications, the mail client issues IDLE, or its successor extension command NOTIFY, and the Lemonade IMAP server sends unsolicited responses over that connection.

Out-of-IMAP (outband) notifications reach the user or client by some other route. When aimed at a person they are readable alerts. When aimed at the client they are machine-readable and the client may fetch data from the mail store, resynchronize mailboxes, update state or alert the user. Outband notifications are usually wanted only when the client is not connected over IMAP, so it helps if the mail system tells the notification system when the user logs in or out.

Good push email needs the client to be informed when interesting events happen so it can connect and resynchronize.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are already on the phone with the mail server, it just whispers the news to you. If you are not, a separate message taps you on the shoulder.

sections.title: Server-to-Server Notifications
sections.content:
With server-to-server notifications, the mail system sends state change events to a notification system. Each event describes one mailbox event, such as the arrival of a new message or a full mailbox. The notification system holds the user and client preferences and decides what alerts to send, perhaps by SMS, WAP Push or instant message. That last hop is out of scope.

The RFC groups notification systems into three styles: external smart clients that poll or listen, intrinsic notification inside the mail system (for example Sieve notifications), and separate notification systems. The separate style is architecturally cleaner, since the mail system supports one extra protocol and does not track who wants what, and it can serve email, voicemail and other services alike. The cost is a new service and an additional protocol.

Sieve notifications are noted as a fairly easy and quick deployment option, because many mail systems already support Sieve.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every mailbox knowing how to reach you, they all tell one messenger service what happened, and the messenger knows how you like to be told.

sections.title: Event Order and Reliability
sections.content:
For the Lemonade Profile, event order is generally not important. Notifications can carry a modification sequence identifier (modseq), so a client can tell whether it has already handled the triggering event, for instance when a notification arrives late or after a resynchronization. Lost or delayed notifications are tolerated, because the client can resynchronize when it next connects.

Generic server-to-server notifications are different. The order is likely to matter, so the mail system needs to deliver events in the order they occurred. The data in a state change event is assumed to be important, so a high level of reliability is needed between the mail system and any external notification system.
sections.plainLanguage: If your phone misses a buzz, it can just check the mailbox next time. But a messenger service needs every report, in the right order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Notification content needs protection against eavesdropping and alteration when it contains specifics such as the sender. Even trivial notifications may need the sender to be authenticated or verified, to guard against denial-of-service attacks.

Protocols that change filters need protection against modification and disclosure by unauthorized parties. A malicious entity might delete notifications the user wants, or flood a device with notifications to run up usage charges. The filters themselves may reveal email addresses and relationships between people or organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes about your mail should not be readable or fakeable by strangers, and nobody should be able to flood your phone with buzzes.
